principles: Legend first, ledger second — the smirk comes before the footnote
Professional at first glance, playful on second read
Prefer euphemism and corporate jargon over explicit criminal language
Names should feel like 2026 LinkedIn, not 1739 parish records
Victorian myth (Black Bess, Ainsworth romance) is fair game as in-universe marketing lore
Mark wholly invented personas and events clearly
Prefer witty understatement over overt criminal glorification

examples.good: Richard Turpin — CEO, Strategic Corridor Operations. Known internally for aggressive route optimisation across the Home Counties.
examples.bad: Born in Hempstead, Essex, Turpin began as a butcher before turning to smuggling and highway robbery.
examples.reason: Lead with the modern persona and corporate euphemism; historical detail is optional colour.

examples.good: Rose & Crown Hospitality — where discretion is part of the room rate.
examples.bad: Historic coaching inn providing premium accommodation, intelligence services, and hospitality management.
examples.reason: Organisation descriptions should land a punchline, not read like a brochure.

examples.good: Case #0042: Palmer/Palmer identity collision in SSO — two active accounts, one Yorkshire postcode.
examples.bad: Turpin used a fake name lol and got caught.
examples.reason: Cases sound like real tickets that reward a second read.

examples.good: Ned Palmer, Identity Management Consultant — provisions SSO credentials for Yorkshire relocations.
examples.bad: Guy who helped Dick with fake papers.
examples.reason: Job titles do the heavy lifting; biography reinforces the gag.
